20.0.s.en: 1. There is a time for silence and a time for speech

20.0.0.en: (Sir 19:28) There is one that reproveth, and it is not comely; and there is one that holdeth his tongue, and he is wise. 1 How much better is it to reprove, than to be angry secretly! and he that confesseth his fault shall be preserved from hurt. 2 As is the lust of an eunuch to deflower a virgin; so is he that executeth judgment with violence. 3 And so is he who gives an unjust judgment. 4 How good is it, when thou art reproved, to show repentance! for so shalt thou escape wilful sin. 5 There is one that keepeth silence, and is found wise; and another by much babbling becometh hateful. 6 Some man holdeth his tongue, because he hath not to answer; and some keepeth silence, knowing his time. 7 A wise man will hold his tongue till he see opportunity; but a babbler and a fool will regard no time. 8 He that useth many words shall be abhorred; and he that taketh to himself authority therein shall be hated.

20.0.1.en: There is a rebuke that is not in its time, and there is one who keeps silent and has discernment [1].

20.0.2.en: Neither speech nor silence is a virtue or a vice in itself; rather the use of silence or of speech at the proper time and in a manner befitting the sons of the Lord is counted a virtue. For a man may be silent while his heart is not pure, and he may also speak while his heart is not pure.

20.0.3.en: v He who has acquired the truth, Jesus speaks with him, and he is able to listen even to His silence (the silence of the Lord Christ), and so he becomes perfect and acts by His word and His silence (the silence of the believer who is aware of the silence of the Lord Christ) [1].

20.1.0.en: St. Ignatius the God-bearer v Keep away from listening to worldly tales, lest your souls be stained in any way with mire. Do not be eager to hear the words of others, nor to throw yourselves into the discussions of others, so that you do not make yourselves a subject of mockery and cause others to commit slanders [2].

20.2.0.en: St. Basil the Great v Those who are unsteady and untried must not try to subject the wise to mere questioning (their concern should not be merely their asking), for the wise man is one who seeks to please God, and is much in silence, and if he speaks he speaks little, uttering what is necessary and pleasing to God [3].

20.2.1.en: St. Anthony the Great v It is better for you to remain among thousands of men with a loving heart than to hide in caves alone with hatred in you.

20.2.2.en: St. Evagrius How much better is rebuke than raging with anger [2].

20.2.3.en: He who confesses his fault is saved from loss [3].

20.2.4.en: Rebuke with love and wisdom is a declaration of the Church's love for the sinner and her hatred of his sin; therefore the pastor must take care, while rebuking, that:

20.2.5.en: a. It proceed from a fatherly heart full of compassion and meekness (1 Cor 21:4).

20.2.6.en: b. It be given according to the state of the sinner and his capacities, and discipline be offered in a flexible form, not in the form of a rigid law or a dry compulsion.

20.2.7.en: c. Discipline must end in repentance full of hope.

20.2.8.en: v I ask: who among men was more corrupt than the king of Babylon (Nebuchadnezzar)... Many opportunities for repentance were given to him. The first was that miracle which took place in the furnace of fire (that is, the appearance of the Son of God with the three young men in the midst of the fire) (Dan 3). The second was those visions that appeared to him, which Daniel interpreted for him, visions able to crush any heart of stone (Dan 4), and after that the counsels of the prophet himself.

20.2.9.en: In all this God did not punish him but was long-suffering toward him, counseling him at one time by visions and at another by the tongue of His prophet; but since no correction came to him by any of these means, at last He poured punishment upon him: "And he was driven from the sons of men; and his heart was made like the beasts, and his dwelling was with the wild asses: they fed him with grass like oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven" (Dan 5:21). And this punishment was not for vengeance, for He restored him again to his first position without any loss befalling him, but he benefited as greatly as possible.

20.2.10.en: St. John Chrysostom v The Apostle Paul teaches us not to abandon those who have committed a sin unto death, but to bind them to the bread of tears (that is, repentance), yet let their sorrow be moderate. And this is what the phrase means: "Thou hast given them tears to drink by measure" (Ps 130:5); their sorrow must be by measure, lest the penitent be swallowed up by excessive grief. This is as he said to the Corinthians: "What will ye? shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?" (1 Cor 4:21). He uses the rod, but without cruelty, for it is said: "Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell" (Prov 23:14). And what the Apostle means by the rod appeared when he struck against the sin of fornication (1 Cor 5:1), warning against immorality with relatives whom it is forbidden to marry, rebuking their pride, for those who ought to have mourned were puffed up. And finally, speaking of the offender (who wished to marry his father's wife), he commanded that he be removed from the congregation and delivered to Satan, not for the destruction of his soul, but for the destruction of his flesh.

20.3.0.en: St. Ambrose v It is necessary that we confess our sins to those to whom the stewardship of the mysteries of God has been given. Those who showed repentance in ancient times offered it before the saints. It is recorded in the Gospel that they confessed their sins to John the Baptist (Mt 3:6), and in the Book of Acts they confessed to the Apostles, by whom they were also baptized (Acts 19:18) [4].

20.4.0.en: v When you are occupied with some sin, be your own accuser (Prov 18:17), and do not wait for others to bring the accusation. In this way you become like a righteous man who accuses himself in the first words of his speech in court, or like Job, whom the multitude of the people in the city did not hinder from proclaiming his offense before all [5].

20.4.1.en: St. Basil the Great Like the lustful eunuch who deflowers a maiden, so is he who uses violence in carrying out justice [4].

20.4.2.en: For it is impossible for the eunuch to fulfill his desire toward a virgin; he suffers repression and a sense of failure, and he who thinks that he achieves justice by violence fails completely.

20.4.3.en: There is one who keeps silent and is counted wise, and there is a man who is hated for his much speaking [5].

20.4.4.en: He speaks of a person who does not know how to deal with some matter, or does not know the answer to a question put to him; if he admits his ignorance within himself and keeps silent, he is counted wise. But if he tries to answer in order to appear as one who knows, this speech of his makes him hated.

20.5.0.en: There is one who keeps silent because he finds no answer, and one who keeps silent because he knows the proper time for speaking [6].

20.5.1.en: Two keep silent: one because he does not know the answer, and it is wise that he be silent; the second has knowledge but is silent because the time is not suitable for speaking. The latter speaks at the proper time.

20.6.0.en: The wise man keeps silence until the proper time for speaking, but the proud and the foolish miss the proper time for speaking [7].

20.6.1.en: The wise man offers the proper remedy at the proper time, so his word brings fitting fruit; but the proud and the foolish are silent when they ought to speak, as though they do not offer the remedy at the proper time, so they are late in answering, which causes the problem to swell and become complicated.

20.6.2.en: v In truth, when a man sees that what his neighbor is doing is evil and keeps silent, it is as though he withholds the balm from the wounds he sees, and thereby leads him to death, to the extent that they withhold the healing when it was within their power. In this case the tongue should not be completely bound, but we should control it with discretion and wisdom, for it is written: "A wise man will hold his tongue till he see opportunity (but a babbler and a fool will regard no time)" (see Sir 20:7). That is, when speaking what is fitting is suitable, the restraint of silence must be removed and one must speak so that help may be given with every effort. And it is also written: "A time to keep silence, and a time to speak" (Eccl 3:7), meaning that there are various times about which we must think wisely [6].

20.6.4.en: v Now what must we learn before everything else except silence, so that we may be able to speak? Lest my voice condemn me before anything else acquits me, as it is written: "By thy words thou shalt be condemned" (Mt 12:37).

20.6.5.en: What do we need that is safer than keeping silence, that we may hasten to guard against the condemnation that comes through speech? How many I have seen fall into sin through speech, while scarcely anyone falls through silence. And so it is much harder to know how to keep silence than how to speak. It is very rare for anyone to be silent when speaking is not profitable to him. Finally, the wisdom of God says: "The Lord gave me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season" (Isa 50:4) LXX. Well does Holy Scripture say: "A wise man will hold his tongue until the proper time" (see Sir 20:7) [7].

20.7.0.en: St. Ambrose He that useth many words shall be abhorred, and he who forces himself on others shall be hated [8].

20.7.1.en: After Sirach has dealt with the subject of keeping silence or speaking according to what is profitable, he now points to two kinds of error. The first error is that the person speaks at the proper time and has a good answer, but he repeats the answer for a long while and many times, so his answer does not bear fruit, because the hearer grows weary of the many words. The second error is that the person thrusts himself into the lives of others without being asked to, and so the hearer hates him.

20.8.0.en: 9 There is a sinner that hath good success in evil things; and there is a gain that turneth to loss. 10 There is a gift that shall not profit thee; and there is a gift whose recompense is double. 11 There is an abasement because of glory; and there is that lifteth up his head from a low estate. 12 There is that buyeth much for a little, and repayeth it sevenfold. 13 A wise man by his words maketh him beloved, but the graces of fools shall be poured out. 14 The gift of a fool shall do thee no good; for his eyes are many instead of one. 15 He giveth little, and upbraideth much; he openeth his mouth like a crier. 16 He lendeth today, and asketh it again tomorrow: such a one is a hateful man.

20.8.1.en: Sometimes the outward appearance hides the truth, and a man may even deceive himself or those around him. The experience of failure may drive a man to review himself so that he may walk in a spirit of success in the future, while the life of a man may be shattered by an appearance of success, as happens when he wins a huge sum in a lottery [8].

20.8.2.en: There may be success in the midst of trials, and also a gain that turns into a loss [9].

20.8.3.en: A person may enjoy success or gain, but through his bad conduct his success causes him troubles and leads him into severe trials, and what he gained turns into losses. Therefore it befits a person to know how to meet success or gain with wisdom and study, without haste.

20.8.4.en: v [Be not thou afraid when one is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased] (Ps 49:16) LXX.. This declaration is necessary for the inhabitants of the world, whether for the earthborn or for the sons of men, for the rich as well as the poor. "Be not afraid when a man is made rich"; he says: when you see the unjust become rich and the righteous poor, do not fear for yourself. Let not your mind be alarmed, as though the providence of God did not look upon human affairs, or as though the divine watchfulness extended to some places and not to the whole earth, to care for our affairs. If there is divine providence, it extends to every man in the manner that suits him. The righteous who understand how to use wealth become rich, and the wicked who use wealth as an instrument of their evil must needs be poor.

20.8.5.en: Now, since there are many among the Gentiles and among the earthborn who hold such notions, and because of the apparent contradiction in the distribution of wealth for life, they think that the world is not the work of divine providence.

20.8.6.en: Holy Scripture addresses them in order to calm their unsound emotions from the very beginning. It calls them to listen to the teachings. Certainly it refers in particular only to the poor person when it says: "Be not afraid when a man is made rich." These especially need consolation, that they may not tremble before those in authority. For it says that the rich man has no advantages at his death, since he cannot take his wealth with him. At any rate, he reckons that all he possesses is the enjoyment of it, since his soul thinks itself happy in this life through those who flatter him. But at his death he does not take any of those possessions.

20.8.7.en: It says: he takes only the garment with which he covers his shame, and this, as it seems, is the best that his household offer him when they cover him. He must be content to receive a small piece of ground which they offer him, as those who bury him show compassion toward him, offering it to him for the honor of human nature in general, and not as a special privilege of his own, but for the honor of humanity.

20.8.8.en: So do not be troubled about present things, but wait for that blessed life. For you will see that what befalls the righteous man of poverty and insult and deprivation of luxury is for his good. Do not be troubled now about what you count as goods, that they are distributed as though unjustly. You will hear what will be said to a certain rich man: "Thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things" (Lk 16:25). But for the poor man, evils befell him in this life; therefore the latter is comforted and the former is tormented.

20.8.9.en: [And he will praise thee, when thou doest well to him] (Ps 49:18) LXX. This concerns the earthly man, and him who thinks that goods are the advantages of this life, such as wealth, health and authority that is his own. In truth such a man praises God when he is alone with good things, but in dangerous circumstances he utters curses... So also with the accusations that Satan made against Job (Job 1:9), that Job did not honor God for nothing, but received a reward for his godliness: riches and all the rest of his possessions. Therefore, to prove his virtue, God withdrew all that he had, so that man's thanksgiving toward God might shine through everything [9].

20.9.0.en: St. Basil the Great There is a gift that profits you nothing, and there is a gift that obliges you to repay it double [10].

20.9.1.en: The scholar Origen speaks of the divine gifts to man, some spiritual and others not spiritual. Spiritual gifts support the wise man and build up his soul as they build up others, while non-spiritual gifts may be misused by a man; though they are not evil in themselves, by their wrong use they become evil.

20.9.2.en: A man may gain money and misuse it in a life of luxury, drunkenness or association with the wicked. Another finds in money the opportunity to support his family, his friends and the needy. Therefore it befits us to imitate wise Solomon, who asked neither for money nor glory nor victory over enemies, but that God would grant him wisdom for the governing of the life of the kingdom and of his own life.

20.9.3.en: v When (the Apostle) says: "That I may impart unto you some spiritual gift" (Rom 1:11), he knows that there are gifts that are not spiritual. Certainly the gift of faith is spiritual, and also the gift of wisdom and knowledge and the like, such as virginity. But when he speaks of marriage and virginity he says: "Every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that" (1 Cor 7:7). So in truth he calls marriage a gift, as it is written: "A prudent wife is from the Lord" (Prov 19:14), but this gift is not spiritual. Many other things can also be called gifts from God, such as wealth, bodily strength, outward beauty and earthly kingdoms. For God gives these, as Daniel says: "He removeth kings, and setteth up kings" (Dan 2:21), but these gifts are not spiritual [10].

20.9.4.en: The scholar Origen Some gifts and talents may profit nothing when a man misuses them or uses them in a spirit of pride and arrogance, for God is able to lift up a humble man and bring low a proud man. He raises men from the dunghill and sets them with the nobles of His people, as He did with Joseph the son of Jacob (Gen 37-50), and as is recorded in the song of St. Mary (Lk 1:47-53).

20.10.0.en: There is a glory that causes losses, and there is a man who lifts up his head from a state of lowliness [11].

20.10.1.en: Many fell into pride because of their temporal glory, so the Lord brought them down from their thrones, and they even lost their eternity, while the Lord lifted up the heads of the humble. "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree" (Lk 1:52).

20.10.2.en: v Great is the power of this medicine, and great the strength of this comparison, in the healing of the disease of pride. Why are you puffed up? Or why does another despise himself? Are we not all one body, the great among us and the small? If in our totality we are one, and members one of another, why do you isolate yourself by haughtiness? Why do you insult your brother? For as he is a member of you, you are a member of him. (The Apostle) has established two things that break the proud spirit: the first, that we are members one of another, not only the small a member of the great but the great also of the small; and the second, that we are one body. Indeed there is a third point, that the gift is from grace, so do not be proud, for it is given to you from God...

20.10.3.en: Also when he touches on the subject of gifts, he does not say that one is greater and another smaller, but what? The gifts are different! His words are thus: "Having then gifts" (Rom 12:6) are not less and greater but "differing [11]".

20.11.0.en: St. John Chrysostom There is one who buys much for little, but he pays for it sevenfold [12].

20.11.1.en: What is mentioned here is suffered by many, since some are preoccupied with buying what they need at the lowest possible price, without a right estimate of what they lose through this choice of theirs. Examples of this:

20.11.2.en: a. A man buys an old building and tries to repair and maintain it, considering the price less than the price of the land itself. And since the buyer is bound to continual repairs, he finds that he has spent on the building many times what he would have paid had he built it or bought a building in good condition.

20.11.3.en: b. We often find some people spending long hours to buy something at the lowest possible price; they have wasted much of their time, and they and their family are in need of time more than of what they saved in the price.

20.11.4.en: c. In choosing the least cost for buying or making something, he may enter into family discussions that spoil the peace of the family, which is beyond price.

20.12.0.en: The wise man makes himself beloved by his words, and the kindness of the fool is forgotten [13].

20.12.1.en: The wise man knows the worth of the sweet word that establishes friendships, but the fool may offer kindness and favors, yet since he does not join the favor to a sweet word, the favor loses its value, and the recipient of the favor no longer remembers it.

20.13.0.en: The gift of the fool will profit you nothing, for he has many eyes instead of one [14].

20.13.1.en: In his folly the fool exaggerates matters, and so he looks at them as with many eyes. An example of this is the unwise mother, who sees in her son the cleverest of men, and in her daughter the most beautiful of girls. Not estimating matters as one ought spoils a person's peace and crushes those around him. At the same time, in his exaggeration the person thinks that he is the source of their success and their wealth, and so on.

20.13.2.en: v The eye is the source of the body's sight, and the mind is the source of the soul's sight. And just as the body is blind without the eyes, so that it does not behold the shining sun upon the earth and the sea, and cannot enjoy its light, so the soul is blind without a sound mind and a good life, so that it has no knowledge of God, nor glorifies the Creator, the maker of good things for all humanity, nor is able to enjoy joy through obtaining incorruption and receiving eternal blessedness [12].

20.13.3.en: St. Anthony the Great He gives little and insults much, and he opens his mouth like a crier.

20.14.0.en: He lends today and demands it tomorrow. Such a man is hateful [15].

20.14.1.en: A warning against the foolish man: if he offers a gift, behind it is a measure of insults. He offers a gift and causes more losses than he gave. In his folly the fool offers very little and counts himself the most giving and generous of men. He always expects from those he deals with words of praise, thanks and honor, by one means or another. His mouth is always open complaining of those around him because they have not honored him as is fitting. His life in his own eyes is losing deals, with none to reward him for his gifts.

20.14.2.en: Such a man is hateful, because he offers little and adds to the offering complaints, grumbling and insults, which causes psychological and spiritual losses both to himself and to the one to whom he gave the offering.

20.15.0.en: 17 A fool will say, I have no friends, I have no thank for all my good deeds, and they that eat my bread speak evil of me. 18 How oft, and of how many, shall he be laughed to scorn! for he knoweth not aright what it is to have; and it is all one unto him as if he had it not. 19 To slip upon a pavement is better than to slip with the tongue: so the fall of the wicked shall come speedily. 20 An unseasonable tale will always be in the mouth of the unwise. 21 A wise sentence shall be rejected when it cometh out of a fool's mouth; for he will not speak it in due season.

20.15.1.en: After speaking of the deceit of outward appearances, and requiring the wise man to study matters with wisdom, deliberation and depth so that he knows the truths and is not deceived, he spoke of man's need for the grace of God, which leads thought inward so that it comes to know the truth. The man who relies on his own understanding and thoughts, stripped of grace, lacks true discernment. However great a man's intelligence, abilities and studies may be, he needs his depths sanctified by divine grace, not to destroy his thought but to elevate it and sanctify it and reveal to it the transcendent mysteries.

20.15.2.en: The fool says: I have no friend, and my good works are not met with thanks [16].

20.15.3.en: Since the ignorant man feels that he has no friend, and that there is none to thank him for his good works, he exerts all his effort to immortalize his name and his memory on earth. He may set up projects that bear witness to his goodness and splendid buildings on which he carves his name. And he does not realize that by his sins he has become dead, cast into the grave. His very body becomes a tomb for his dead soul. St. Basil marvels at those who carve their names on tombs, thus tying their names to death instead of recording them in the book of life. It is as though, having failed to have friends in the heavenly places, they seek friends among the dead. Since the foolish man does not enjoy divine grace nor respond to it, always complaining, he reckons that he is deprived of a faithful friend who would appreciate his good works. He sees that many eat his bread, and instead of offering him thanks they mock him.

20.15.4.en: v "The ignorant and the dull (the foolish, senseless) perish together, and leave their wealth to others. Their tombs are their dwellings from generation to generation; they call their lands by their own names" (Ps 48:10-11) LXX...

20.15.5.en: The senseless is in truth he who lacks common sense, and who has no sound insight into ordinary human affairs. In the same way, those who discern in the affairs of life between what is useful and what is harmful are usually called wise or prudent. This is what is expressed in the Gospel: "For the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light" (Lk 16:8). They are not wise in an absolute way, but because of their shrewdness in managing their present life in the flesh, they are also called servants of unrighteousness. In this sense the wise are also vipers, which prepare hidden places for themselves, and in time of danger avoid by every means the blows falling upon the head.

20.15.6.en: One is called ignorant who lacks the lofty qualities of man. These are the understanding of God the Father, the reception of the Word, Who "was in the beginning with God" (Jn 1:2), and the light that comes from the Holy Spirit.

20.15.7.en: These persons who have this mind are able to say with Paul: "But we have the mind of Christ" (1 Cor 2:16). Nevertheless Holy Scripture uses the opposite, saying that the wicked man is senseless in these words: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God" (Ps 15:1). Again it calls what is harmful to life folly, as the Apostle did in speaking of those who fell into foolish and hurtful lusts (1 Tim 6:9).

20.15.8.en: Thus the senseless and the ignorant go down to one end, which is destruction. And one may say that he who lives like the pagans is called foolish, but he who conducts his life as a Jew with an outward (literal) appearance in keeping the Law is ignorant. For the Lord said to the foolish man because of the godlessness in him: "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Lk 12:20). But Israel, who walked according to the flesh, was called ignorant, as the prophet says: "Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria" (Hos 7:11).

20.15.9.en: Where these perished completely through their ignorance, we strangers have become heirs of their wealth. The commandments became ours, the prophets and the fathers became ours, and so the righteous in the world became ours. These who perished in their ignorance left us their wealth.

20.15.10.en: At any rate, the houses of these foolish and ignorant have become tombs for them forever. For the tombs of those whose lives were filled with dead works of every kind of sin are their houses forever. He who is dead in sins does not dwell in a house but in a tomb, because his soul is dead.

20.15.11.en: Now Jacob, innocent in his conduct and simple, dwelt in a house. It is written of him that he was a plain and good man dwelling in a house (see Gen 25:27), but the base man dwells in a tomb, and lays no foundation for regret, because of his dead works; rather he resembles a sepulchre whitewashed outwardly, very splendid, but within full of dead men's bones and all uncleanness (Mt 23:27). Therefore when such a man speaks, he does not open his mouth with the word of God, but he has a tomb; his throat is an open sepulchre. Therefore if anyone believes in Christ and does not practice his works in harmony with his faith, then since he listens to corrupt teachings and blasphemes the meanings of Holy Scripture, he is shattered upon the rock of his tomb [13].

20.15.12.en: v "Their houses are for ever, their dwelling places to all generations" (Ps 48:12) LXX, that is, their tombs are their houses forever. Then, explaining what he means by tombs, to show that he was speaking of their bodies in which their souls perish through their evils, he adds these words: "their dwelling places to all generations"; for human bodies are always called dwelling places. These also call their lands by their names. For the name of the base man is not recorded in the book of the living, nor is he counted with the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven. Rather their names remain on the earth, since they preferred this passing life of short span to the eternal dwellings. Do you not see how those who build marketplaces and schools in the cities, and set up walls, and construct channels, write their names on earthly buildings?

20.15.13.en: Indeed some have engraved their names on herds of horses, and made plans to extend their memory over a long time in life; they raised splendid buildings for their tombs and engraved their names on monuments. These are the wise in earthly matters, who care for present glory and reckon that men's remembering them is enough to achieve happiness. For if you see any of those who exalt themselves greatly in what they falsely call knowledge, and devote themselves to corrupt teachings which they have approved, and instead of the name of Christians ascribe themselves to one of the heretics: Marcion or Valentinus or one of the contemporaries of the present, devoting themselves to working on behalf of destructive men, and in short in earthly matters [14].

20.15.14.en: St. Basil the Great If the foolish do not gain friends for themselves, it is because they do not understand the meaning of true friendship.

20.15.15.en: St. John Chrysostom often speaks of the love that establishes friends for a man. If he establishes ten friends together, then instead of having two hands with which to work, he has all the hands, that is, twenty-two hands with which each one of them works; how much more if by love he gains thousands to work with him, and they work with him.

20.15.16.en: v Do you perceive the loftiness of love, how it makes one man who cannot be conquered increase many times over what he is? Do you not see that one man can be present in many places at one time (since each friend of his is counted as though he were himself)? A part of him will be in Persia as in Rome.

20.15.17.en: What is there that love cannot do? A part of him is present here and another there. Or rather, the whole is here and the whole is there. If he has a thousand friends, or two thousand, imagine again the extent of his strength... (do you not see that love multiplies a man's strength?) It is remarkable that one man carries a thousand of his strength [15].

20.15.18.en: St. John Chrysostom Those who eat my bread, their speech is without benefit.

20.15.19.en: How many are those who mock him! And in many ways! [17]

20.15.20.en: These are the feelings of the fool, for since he walks in malice he thinks of those to whom he does good that instead of thanks they speak against him with a malicious tongue.

20.16.0.en: A slip on the ground is better than a slip of the tongue; so the fall of the wicked will be swift [18].

20.16.1.en: Why is the error of the tongue called a "slip"? Because what the fool utters is an unconscious reaction of his folly. The fool errs with his tongue without thinking, but the effect of this slip is grave, and may extend to the great day of the Lord, unless he has offered true repentance for it. It seems as though a slip of the tongue is talk in the air that is of no danger, but Sirach likens it to falling on a pavement, causing him fractures, and it can cause a rupture in the arteries of the brain leading to his death.

20.16.2.en: v The soundness of the tongue is the tree of life. The tongue that does not err in speech uses soundness of mind. In truth the disease of the tongue is sin. He who is able to control his tongue and not sin is full of the Holy Spirit [16].

20.17.0.en: St. John Chrysostom The man who has lost grace is like a story told at the wrong time; it continues on the lips of the ignorant [19].

20.17.1.en: The story of the fool who has lost grace is repeated by the ignorant, but the wise man desires the salvation of the fool by his returning to God before it is too late. We notice in Ben Sira that he often repeats "the proper time"; now is the day of salvation and a proper time for repentance, but postponement is folly, because we do not own tomorrow. He realizes that the one who walks by divine grace is able to study and examine everything, and to deal with others with wisdom, dignity and esteem for them. But the one who has lost grace falls into ignorance and makes light of the commandment of God, while not esteeming those around him.

20.17.2.en: The one who has lost grace, in his ignorance, does not accept the control of the tongue, the control of the passions and self-control; he does not accept the divine commandment, nor the sincere order of society, nor the experience of godly elders. Ben Sira defines the fool as a man who has lost grace, who may utter words of wisdom that come out of his lips but without experience.

20.18.0.en: The proverb is rejected from the mouth of the fool, because he does not utter it at the proper time [20].

20.18.1.en: Since the fool does not return to God that He may grant him the grace of repentance, all his words are counted as offered at an unfitting time.

20.18.2.en: The wicked cannot bear witness to the righteous, nor can his testimony be effective.

20.19.0.en: 23 There is that is hindered from sinning through want, and in his rest he shall not be pricked. 24 There is that destroyeth his own soul through bashfulness, and by accepting of persons overthroweth himself. 25 There is that for bashfulness promiseth to his friend, and maketh him his enemy for nothing. 26 A lie is a foul blot in a man, yet it is continually in the mouth of the untaught. 27 A thief is better than a man that is accustomed to lie: but they both shall have destruction to heritage. 28 The disposition of a liar is dishonorable, and his shame is ever with him.

20.19.1.en: There is one whom his want hinders from sin, and in his rest sorrow will not pierce him [21].

20.19.2.en: God allows some to have want or sickness or any tribulation that keeps them from practicing sin, whereas if they were at ease they would not practice repentance and remorse for sin but would walk in slackness and negligence.

20.19.3.en: There is one who loses his life from shame, or loses it because of his foolish conduct [22].

20.19.4.en: Some people are put to shame by what they commit, but they do not set out to repentance in a spirit of joyful hope.

20.19.5.en: There is one who gives a promise to his friend out of shame, and so gains him as an enemy without cause [23].

20.19.6.en: Some make promises to their friends while knowing their inability to fulfill them, but they make them because of shame. And when the time comes to fulfill the promise, friends turn into enemies.

20.20.0.en: A lie is a shameful evil in a man, and it continues on the lips of the ignorant [24].

20.20.1.en: A lie is considered a stain of disgrace on the character; it arises for many reasons, the most important of which is fear, especially in childhood, when the child wishes to escape the punishment imposed on him; or because of a feeling of inferiority, so that he wishes to appear other than he is. If the lie is discovered, many lose confidence in him in all that he says or appears to be. Satan is called the liar and the father of liars (Jn 8:44). Since the Lord Christ is "the Truth" (Jn 14:6), a lie, which is against the truth, is a mark of the "antichrist." Origen says: [The lie points to the adversary of Him who said: "I am the truth" (Jn 14:6). This is the antichrist, whose father is a liar, being the devil [17].]

20.20.2.en: v Everyone must give great attention lest "lying" rob him, for the liar is not united with God. The liar is a stranger to God. And Scripture says that the liar is of Satan, since he is "a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 44:8). Thus Satan was called the father of liars, but the truth is God, for He Himself says: "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (Jn 6:14).

20.20.3.en: Do you not see, then, how we become strangers to God by lying, and with whom we are united (through it)?! Therefore, if we truly wish to be saved, we must love the truth with all our strength and all our zeal, and guard ourselves from every lie, lest it separate us from the truth and the life [18].

20.20.4.en: Father Dorotheus St. Basil deals with the subject of lying in his answers to questions that appear in the Short Rules.

20.20.5.en: v Question: Is he condemned who lies deliberately only, or also he who utters something contrary to the truth out of ignorance on his part?

20.20.6.en: Answer: The judgment of the Lord is also against those who sin out of obvious ignorance, from His saying: "He that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes" (Lk 12:48). And in every case repentance carries the sure hope of forgiveness (Mt 3:8; Lk 3:8) [19]

20.20.7.en: v Question: If someone only thought to do something and did not do it, is this judged to be a lie (1 Tim 1:10)?

20.20.8.en: Answer: If what he thought to do is not according to the commandment, the Holy Spirit condemns him not only as a liar but as disobedient, because God searches the hearts and reins (Ps 7:10) [20]

20.20.9.en: v Question: If someone decided beforehand to do something that is hateful to God, but refrained from doing it, does he cancel his evil decision, or does he complete the sin for fear of being accused of being a liar?

20.20.10.en: Answer: First: it befits such a man to repent first, because in this he dared and decided by himself to do something, whatever it was (without seeking the counsel of God); he must not do even what is good of himself on his own responsibility.

20.20.11.en: Second: what is more serious is that he was not afraid to take a decision that does not please God.

20.20.12.en: As for his having drawn back from what he decided beforehand in opposition to the commandment of the Lord, and not carrying out the decision in practice, this is clear in the case of the Apostle Peter, who decided beforehand and declared: "Thou shalt never wash my feet" (Jn 13:8). And when he heard the judgment that the Lord pronounced: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me," he said... "Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head" (Jn 13:9) [21].

20.20.13.en: v Question: Is there a special exception through which one may lie for the sake of an expected benefit?

20.20.14.en: Answer: This cannot be overlooked by the law of the Lord, Who says entirely that a lie is of Satan (Jn 8:44), without distinguishing between one lie and another. There is also the testimony of the Apostle, where it is written: "And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully" (2 Tim 2:5) [22].

20.21.0.en: St. Basil the Great A thief is better than one who lies continually, but both inherit destruction [25].

20.21.1.en: St. John Chrysostom says: ["Let him that stole steal no more," this does not remove the sin, but how is it removed? If they work, and practice relations of love with others! He does not want us merely to work but to work and toil, that we may practice friendly relations with others. For the thief also has works, but they are evil works [23].]

20.22.0.en: The state of the lying man brings disgrace, and his shame is with him continually [26].

20.23.s.en: 5. The ways of the wise man

20.23.0.en: 29 A wise man shall advance himself to honor with his words, and he that hath understanding will please great men. 30 He that tilleth his land shall increase his heap, and he that pleaseth great men shall get pardon for iniquity. 31 Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise, and stop up his mouth that he cannot reprove. 32 Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is hoarded up, what profit is in them both? 33 Better is he that hideth his folly than a man that hideth his wisdom.

20.23.1.en: The wise man exalts himself by his words, and the prudent man pleases the great [27].

20.23.2.en: We can realize how effective our speech is, for it is said: "By thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned" (Mt 12:37). The Lord Christ says: "Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man" (Mt 15:11). And the wise man says also: "Make... a door and a bar for thy mouth" (see Sir 28:29).

20.23.3.en: St. John Chrysostom speaks of the control of the tongue, saying: [A golden vessel is not used for base things because of the greatness of its price; how much more the mouth, which is more precious than gold and coral, so it is not right for us to defile it with ugly speech, cursing and stabbing others.]

20.23.4.en: And Father John of Kronstadt says: [Take care of your words, for the word is precious!... Utter the creative word of God, for the Word of God is the cause of all creation, in Him are the present, the past and the future [24].] He also says: [If you are speaking with your neighbor, speak with discretion and dignity and in a constructive way, avoiding every idle word as the venom of the serpent [25].]

20.23.5.en: He who tills the land increases his harvest, and he who pleases the great atones for the fault [28].

20.23.6.en: If the abundant harvest is the fruit of effort and toil in tilling the land, then the kind word that pleases the great rescues the wronged.

20.23.7.en: Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise, and like a bridle in the mouth they prevent rebuke [29].

20.23.8.en: St. John Chrysostom warns us of envy, which pierces even the Church and corrupts it with covetousness, since envy is the mother of covetousness, and presents and gifts move its affairs.

20.23.9.en: v (Envy) has pierced into the Church. From the beginning it brings countless grave results. It is the mother of covetousness, and the plague that turns matters upside down and corrupts justice. Scripture says: "Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise, and like a bridle in the mouth prevent rebukes" (see Sir 20:29). Covetousness makes us slaves instead of being free. We speak of it every day, but we make no progress [26].

20.23.10.en: St. John Chrysostom Gifts that are offered as a bribe corrupt the sight of the wise and bridle their mouths, so that they are prevented from rebuking the wrongdoer, and cannot behold the truth. And they stop the mouths, so that they do not rebuke the unjust and the wicked; but being occupied with heavenly things and divine gifts opens the eyes to see the mysteries of God and to perceive the divine truth, as it opens the mouths to praise with the angels, and to rebuke the devil and all his powers, and not to flatter the wicked.

20.23.11.en: v This (love of fame and money) has rushed into the churches. This is the cause of countless deadly things from the beginning. This is the father of covetousness. This disease has turned all things upside down and corrupted justice. It is said: "Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise, and like a bridle in the mouth prevent rebukes" (see Sir 20:29). This has made free men slaves. Of this we speak every day without benefit. We have become worse than the wild beasts, we plunder orphans, strip widows, sin against the poor, and add woe to woe. "Woe! The godly man is perished out of the earth" (Mic 7:1) [27].

20.23.12.en: St. John Chrysostom v A chorepiscopus asked St. Barsanuphius whether he should leave his episcopal work and withdraw to a monastery, and the answer came: I cannot advise you to abandon Him Who entrusted you to care for the holy churches of God (2 Cor 11:28), but to care for your own soul according to the fear of God. Do not accept gifts from anyone (see Sir 20:29; Prov 15:27). Do not hesitate in your judgments (Ex 23:3). Do not be ashamed to appear before any ruler (see Sir 7:6). Do not acquit the guilty, and do not condemn the righteous. Keep covetousness far from you, for it is the root of all evil (1 Tim 6:10)... Do not be proud but be led by the humble (Rom 12:16)... Remember the day of your departure, and then you will not sin against the Lord (see Sir 7:36). And if you reach the point of stillness, you will find rest with grace wherever you withdraw [28].
